summary: Vint Cerf's notes on how the IMP operating system controlled traffic flow in 1972, based on a BBN meeting. The goals included fewer needless retransmissions under heavy load and keeping reassembly from locking up. It is an informal account, and RFC 449 offers corrections and better references.

plainLanguage.summary: A traffic cop for network messages that keeps roads from jamming. This note is one person's description of how the cop decided who may go.

subtitle: Vint Cerf's notes on how IMPs reserve buffer space, order messages and acknowledge packets to control traffic.

tldr.problem: The IMP network needed to avoid needless retransmissions under heavy load, avoid waiting for a retransmission time-out under light load, increase bandwidth, and prevent re-assembly lock-up.
tldr.mechanism: A source IMP asks the destination IMP to reserve buffer space before sending (8 packets for multi-packet messages), messages carry numbers so they can be ordered, and acknowledgments ride in a single bit of packets flowing the other way.
tldr.outcome: This is one author's understanding of a meeting, and RFC 449 is listed as updating it.

today: The metadata lists no formal status for RFC 442, and it says the note is updated by RFC 449. The text is one author's understanding of a 1972 meeting and not a formal specification.

sections.title: Goals of the Scheme
sections.content:
BB&N quarterly report #13 outlined part of the flow control scheme in the IMP operating system, and a meeting on March 16, 1972 at BB&N described it to interested participants. Vint Cerf writes up his understanding of it here.

The goals are to eliminate unnecessary retransmissions when the load is heavy, eliminate the retransmission time-out period when the load is light, increase bandwidth, prevent re-assembly lock-up, and control traffic from hosts into the net more strictly than the earlier link blocking method. (The list ends with a joke about life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.)
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is a smoother road: fewer repeats when it is busy, no pointless waiting when it is quiet, and no jams at the end.

sections.title: Source IMP to Destination IMP
sections.content:
There are two protocols, depending on whether a message is one packet or several. A single packet message acts as an implicit request for one packet of buffer space. If there is room, the destination replies with a RFNM and the source discards its saved copy. If there is no room, the destination records the request in a first-come-first-served queue and later sends an ALL (1); the source then sends the message again, knowing space is reserved.

For a multi-packet message, the source IMP halts the host-to-IMP line when the first full packet has arrived without the last bit flag, and sends REQ (8). When 8 buffers are free the destination answers ALL (8). The source sends the message and waits for a combined RFNM and ALL (8); the destination delays its RFNM, if needed, until it has another 8 buffers for the next multi-packet message.

Time-outs back this up. The source resends REQ (8) after 30 seconds, the destination resets unused reservations after 2 minutes, and a source that receives an allocation has 125 ms to start the transfer. A source that gets no response sends an INC? query.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like booking a table before you bring a big group to a restaurant. If the restaurant has no room it writes your name down and calls when a table is free.

sections.title: Buffers and Message Ordering
sections.content:
A total of 40 buffers serve store-and-forward and re-assembly. At most 32 can be allocated for re-assembly and at most 24 to 25 for store-and-forward, so neither kind of traffic can shut out the other.

An IMP can have at most 4 messages outstanding (not yet RFNMed) for each other IMP. The IMPs ignore link numbers and instead mark messages with an 8-bit message number, plus a 2-bit priority number when a host marked the message as priority. All hosts at one IMP are treated as a single host, with one sequence per pair of sites. The receiver uses these numbers to deliver messages in order, though a slow host can delay messages for other hosts at the same site. Cerf warns that giving a short message priority arbitrarily can reorder a file at the receiving host.
sections.plainLanguage: Each package gets a number so the receiver can put them back in order. The receiver also keeps some shelf space for each kind of job so one kind cannot use up everything.

sections.title: Acknowledging Packets with ODD/EVEN Bits
sections.content:
The IMPs treat each phone line as a pair of one-way paths. Each sender and receiver module holds an ODD/EVEN (OE) bit. Every packet carries an OE bit and an ACK bit. The sender sets POE from its send bit and ACK from its receive bit. A sender that sees ACK different from its send bit does nothing; when they match it flips the bit and frees the channel. A receiver that sees a packet whose OE bit equals its own receive bit discards it as a duplicate; otherwise it flips its bit.

In the new system acknowledgments are a single bit in packets going the other way, rather than separate packets. If no real packet is waiting, a fake packet carries the ACK but is not itself acknowledged. In fact there are 8 OE bits per module, so up to 8 packets can be outstanding, and one packet can acknowledge up to 8. Packets are chosen for sending in this order: priority packets, non-priority packets, unacknowledged packets, others. A 125 ms time-out forces retransmission of old packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Each letter carries a tiny flag that says whether you got the last one. The flag rides along on the mail going the other way, so no extra trips are needed.
